..
KEY MESSAGE 1: Wednesday and Thanksgiving Day look increasingly
cool and wet, and mountain snow showers may arrive by Friday.


Tomorrow will bring fair weather across the region as high  
pressure settles north of the area across the Northeast. This 
will lead to wedging building in across the region with 
northeast flow advecting cool air into the area tomorrow and 
Wednesday. 

Heading into Wednesday, a complex upper level pattern will lead 
to unsettled weather through the Thanksgiving holiday across the
region. Two upper level shortwave features, with one across the
Gulf states, and another across the central Conus look to aid 
in the development of a rather strong surface low off the coast 
of Florida on Wednesday. The upper level shortwave across the 
Gulf looks to become negatively tilted as it enters the northern
Gulf, and will provide significant upper level forcing for 
ascent and divergence aloft along the baroclinic zone off the 
east coast of the US. This will quickly deepen the surface low 
as it tracks north into the Carolinas. As this occurs, the 
second upper level shortwave trough looks to enter the middle 
Mississippi valley by Thursday morning, and is also expected to 
become negatively tilted by this point. Not only will this 
continue to aid in deepening the surface low, which should be 
over North Carolina, but it will also possibly pull the surface 
low slightly to the northwest as it deepens and tracks northward
with time. This is where models differ slightly as the ECMWF 
model wants to bring the surface low more along the leading edge
of the aforementioned wedge front across eastern North 
Carolina, but the GFS has been consistent on bringing this low 
slightly more inland towards central North Carolina. The ECMWF 
model does bring the low westward towards central North Carolina
and Virginia; however, it occurs later in the day on 
Thanksgiving. 

This is mostly due to the timing differences of both models with 
the upper level features as they progress through the region. 
Regardless, this low pressure system will likely impact the 
region with strong winds and heavy rainfall starting late 
Wednesday night and all day Thursday. 

Another uncertainty is how much wind will be able to mix down  
to the surface ahead of the surface low on Wednesday night into 
Thursday as the Wedge will likely lead to an inversion/stable 
layer. While the easterly/southeasterly LLJ is expected to be
around 60-70 knots, it will be a battle to mix this winds down;
however, with the low tracking in close proximity to the area,
the pressure gradient will be quite tight across the region.
This will inevitably lead to strong and gusty northeast winds
starting overnight Wednesday, and continuing into Thursday
evening.  

By Thursday night, the low is expected to lift north of the
region, and winds will transition to westerly/northwesterly
across the area as the aforementioned upper level shortwave 
trough pushes east over the region. This will will lead to some
upslope rain/snow showers across SE West Virginia and SW 
Virginia Thursday night into Friday. As winds transition, an 
850mb northwesterly LLJ in the 40-50 knot range looks to develop
over the region, which will likely mix down to the surface 
leading to a gusty shopping day for many on Friday. 

Regardless of the wind, precipitation totals look impressive
with this system as NBM probabilities of seeing 2.0 inches or 
greater for areas along and east of the Blue Ridge are currently
in the 50-70% range. There is also a 70-95% chance for most of 
the area to see greater than 1.0 inches of precipitation with 
this system. While there is a small chance for nuisance 
flooding with this system from recently fallen leaves clogging 
drainage flows, the overall threat for flooding remains somewhat
low given the ongoing drought concerns and weeks with little to
no rainfall across the region. 

Calmer weather looks to return for the weekend as high pressure
settles south of the region through Sunday.
